errors.problem: indefinite form of the maqṣūr noun مَقْهَى: the tanwīn is placed after the alif maqṣūra and the هـ carries no fatḥa; the standard vocalised spelling is مَقْهًى (fatḥatān on the هـ, then ى). The transliteration maqhan is right, so the learner only sees an oddly written word, but it is the first time the dual-fatḥa on a maqṣūr noun appears
errors.alsoChange: segs[4] word to مَقْهًى; transliteration stays maqhan

errors.problem: day 18 teaches حَارّ in the sense 'spicy' (sentences[1], dialogue.lines[6]-[8], seg gloss 'hot, spicy'); the tap gloss on the quiz option gives only the weather sense from day 16, so a learner tapping the distractor is told the word means hot weather in a lesson about tastes
errors.alsoChange: shared tap glossary entry for حَارّ → 'hot (weather); spicy (food)' so both days read correctly

errors.problem: engine: the Arabic الشَّاي is correct, but the transliteration renders the final unvowelled yāʾ after ā as a vowel: 'sh-shāī' (also 'bi-n-naʿnāʿ … sh-shāī', 'hal … ash-shāī', 'nashrabu sh-shāī l-ān'). The word is shāy; when the content writes a sukūn (شَايْ, وَالشَّايْ in day 16) the engine gives the right 'shāy'. Either the engine should treat ـَاي as āy, or the content should write الشَّايْ consistently
errors.fix: engine rule: final ي after fatḥa + alif with no vowel = y (shāy), or write الشَّايْ in day11 sentences[1], dialogue.lines[4], quiz[2] and day12 dialogue.lines[14]

errors.problem: engine: when a proclitic وَ / لِ is attached to a proper noun the transliteration capitalises the proclitic and lower-cases the name: 'Wadānyāl', 'Walaylā', 'Wasāmī', 'Walubnān', 'Lisāmī', 'Lidānyāl', 'Liyūsuf', 'Wayūsuf'. ALA-LC is wa-Dānyāl, li-Sāmī (compare the engine's own 'wa-Amrīkā', 'wa-l-Qāhira'). The same code path writes 'liʾarbaʿa' (day17 dialogue.lines[0]) where elsewhere a hyphen is used ('wa-abyaḍ')
errors.fix: engine: keep the proper noun capitalised and hyphenate the proclitic (wa-Laylā, li-Sāmī, li-arbaʿa)

errors.current: What happens to ة in the dual?
errors.problem: engine: a bare letter ة inside English prose is transliterated as 'A / at' ('What happens to A / at in the dual?', 'drop A / at and add -āt', 'it ends in A / at, so the adjective takes a / at too'). If the romanised view is shown to the learner these grammar explanations become unreadable; the Arabic text is fine. Similar glitches: mid-sentence capitals on endings ('Add -Āni to the noun', 'add -Ūna', '-Īna')
errors.fix: engine: render a standalone ة as 'tāʾ marbūṭa (-a/-at)' or leave the letter in Arabic; do not capitalise a transliterated suffix that starts a tap token mid-sentence

notes.note: هَلْ تَشْرَبِينَ الشَّايَ أَمِ الْقَهْوَةَ؟ — prescriptive grammars pair the alternative أَمْ with the hamza question (أَتَشْرَبِينَ الشَّايَ أَمِ الْقَهْوَةَ؟), not with هَلْ. هَلْ … أَمْ is extremely common in modern MSA and will be understood, so this is a register note, not an error; day16 dialogue.lines[4] and [6] use أَمْ after كَيْفَ / مَاذَا, which is fine.

هَيَّا يَا أَصْدِقَاء، نَشْرَبُ الشَّاي الْآن translated 'let's drink our tea now': the Arabic is the plain indicative 'we drink'. With هَيَّا it reads naturally as a suggestion, so it is acceptable here; the explicit 'let's' form (لِنَشْرَبْ) can wait until the imperative/jussive is taught.

عَلِي is written without the shadda on the final yāʾ (standard عَلِيّ). Consistent across the day and the transliteration ʿAlī is right, so per the brief it is not reported as an error; worth normalising when the shared name list is touched.
tap gloss مَاءً=water lacks the '(object)' label that every other -an word in the chunk carries (shāyan, qahwatan, bāridan). Cosmetic consistency only.

tap gloss تَأْكُلُ=she eats: the same form is glossed 'you eat (to a man)' in sentences[2]. Both are correct readings of تَأْكُلُ; a gloss 'you eat (to a man) / she eats' would avoid a learner thinking they are different words.

Fatima calls Daniel يَا حَبِيبِي: correct and warm Egyptian usage from an older woman to a young guest; the 'my darling' gloss may surprise an English speaker, so the seg's '(to a man)' could add 'affectionate, also to children and young guests'.

summary: Checked every Arabic string in days 11-20 (sentences, mistakes pairs, dialogues, readings, titles, culture notes, all quiz prompts, options and answer keys) for harakat, case endings, verb conjugation (present-tense prefixes and the -īna/-ūna/-āni/-ayni endings), gender/number agreement including the feminine-singular rule for plurals of things and the gender polarity of numbers 3-10 (سَبْعَة صُحُون, سَبْعَ مَلَاعِق, عَشَرَة أَرْغِفَة, عَشْر كَلِمَات, ثَلَاثَة أَكْوَاب all correct), the sun/moon assimilation, every seg and tap gloss, the English translations and literals, and the transliteration against the Arabic. The chunk is clean: no major errors, no wrong answer key, no wrong verb form or agreement anywhere. Five minor findings: one orthographic (مَقْهىً should be written مَقْهًى), one tap gloss out of sense (حَارّ glossed 'hot (weather)' in the tastes lesson), and three systematic engine issues (الشَّاي rendered 'shāī' unless a sukūn is written; proclitic + name capitalised as 'Wadānyāl'/'Lisāmī'; a bare ة in English prose rendered 'A / at', which makes several grammar explanations unreadable in the romanised view). Six notes on register and consistency (هَلْ … أَمْ, indicative used for 'let's', عَلِي without shadda, two gloss-label inconsistencies, حَبِيبِي).
